source_text: Fragmenta in epistulam ad Romanos Rom 7 Ἀγαθοεργῶν ὁ θεῖος ἀπόστολος εἰκὼν ἀκηλίδωτος ἐγίνετο τῶν μαθητευομένων, ὅτου χάριν καὶ ἐκέκραξεν· μιμηταί μου γίνεσθε, καθὼς καὶ ἐγὼ Χριστοῦ. τοιγαροῦν οὐκ αὐτοῦ ἐστι κατὰ κυριολεξίαν ὃ ἔφη· οἶδα δὲ ὅτι οὐκ οἰκεῖ ἐν τῇ σαρκί μου τὸ ἀγαθόν, ἀλλ' οὐδὲ τὸ ταλαίπωρος ἐγὼ ἄνθρωπος, τίς με ῥύσεται ἐκ τοῦ σώματος τοῦ θανάτου τούτου; ἀλλὰ ταῦτα καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα ἐν παρενθέτῳ προσώπῳ ὑποκρινόμενος λέγει πρὸς ἔλεγχον τῶν φιλαμαρτημόνων. ὥσπερ δὲ τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἀπὸ τῶν σφῶν πράξεων σαρκικούς, ψυχικούς, πνευματικοὺς καὶ ἑτέροις μυρίοις ὀνόμασι καλεῖν οἶδεν ἡ θεία γραφή, οὕτω δὴ καὶ τὸν διάβολον οὐ μόνον σατανᾶν καὶ ἀντικείμενον καὶ διάβολον καὶ ὄφιν καὶ λέοντα καλεῖν οἶδεν καὶ Βελίαρ, ἀλλὰ γὰρ καὶ σάρκα καὶ νόμον καὶ ἁμαρτίαν καὶ θάνατον· τούτοις γὰρ ἐδουλεύσαμεν διὰ τῆς παρακοῆς καὶ οὐ τῷ Χριστῷ. ὅτου χάριν λέγει· ὅτε ἦμεν ἐν τῇ σαρκί, δηλῶν ὡς νυνὶ οὐκέτι ὄντων αὐτῶν ἐν σαρκί, καίπερ ὄντων ἐν σαρκί, ὡς οὐκ ἄρα τὴν σάρκα ἣν περικείμεθα διαβάλλων, ἀλλὰ τὴν ὁμωνύμως αὐτῇ λεγομένην σάρκα, ἧς καὶ ἀπηλλάγημεν διὰ τὸ ἀποθανεῖν ἡμᾶς ἐν Χριστῷ διὰ τοῦ συνταφῆναι αὐτῷ διὰ τοῦ βαπτίσματος. ὄντως ταύτης ἠλευθερώθημεν τῆς σαρκός· ἐπιφέρει γὰρ λέγων· νυνὶ δὲ κατηργήθημεν ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου τῆς ἁμαρτίας, ἀποθανόντες ἐν ᾧ κατειχόμεθα, ὥστε δουλεύειν ἡμᾶς ἐν καινότητι πνεύματος καὶ οὐ παλαιότητι γράμματος. εἰθ' οὕτως ἤρξατο πάλιν τῆς καθ' ὑπόθεσιν προσωποποιΐας, ἀρξάμενος ἀπὸ τοῦ τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν; ὁ νόμος ἁμαρτία; μὴ γένοιτο· ἕως τοῦ ταλαίπωρος ἐγὼ ἄνθρωπος, τίς με ῥύσεται ἐκ τοῦ σώματος τοῦ θανάτου τούτου; ἄσειστον θεμέλιον προθέμενος ἐν προλόγῳ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἀπολογίαν οὕτω λέγων· τί οὖν; ὁ νόμος ἁμαρτία; μὴ γένοιτο, καὶ ὅτι ὁ μὲν 2 νόμος ἅγιος, καὶ ἡ ἐντολὴ ἁγία καὶ δικαία καὶ ἀγαθή. ἐνταῦθα νόμον λέγει οὐ τὸν ἀντιστρατευόμενον τῷ νόμῳ τοῦ νοὸς ἡμῶν, ἀλλὰ τὸν προπαραινετικόν, τὸν τοὺς ἁμαρτάνοντας κολάζοντα. ὅτου χάριν καὶ συνεψηφίσατο αὐτῷ ὡς ὁσίῳ καὶ δικαίῳ καὶ ἀγαθῷ. εἰθ' οὕτως ἤρξατο πάλιν ἐπιλύειν ἀκολούθως οἷς ἀνωτέρω προεῖπεν, λόγον εὐχάριστον προοιμιασάμενος οὕτως· εὐχαριστῶ τῷ θεῷ διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν. εἶτα πρὸς κατάκρισιν τῶν τοιάδε ἀφορμαζομένων καὶ κακιζόντων ἃς περικείμεθα σάρκας, λέγει ἐπερωτηματικῶς ἆρα οὖν αὐτὸς ἐγὼ τῷ μὲν νοῒ δουλεύω νόμῳ θεοῦ, τῇ δὲ σαρκὶ νόμῳ ἁμαρτίας; ἆρα κἀγὼ Παῦλος μεμέρισμαι, πῆ μὲν δουλεύων νόμῳ θεοῦ, πῆ δὲ νόμῳ ἁμαρτίας; ἆρα τὸν Χριστὸν καὶ τὸν Βελίαρ ἅμα καὶ κατὰ τὸ αὐτὸ ἔχω ἐν ἐμαυτῷ; ἆρα ἐγὼ ὁ λέγων· ζῶ δὲ οὐκέτι ἐγώ, ζῇ δὲ ἐν ἐμοὶ Χριστός, ψευσάμενος τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ζῶσαν ἔχω ἐν ἐμαυτῷ; ὁ ἄλλοις προσφωνήσας· οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι τὰ σώματα ὑμῶν ναὸς τοῦ ἐν ὑμῖν ἁγίου πνεύματός ἐστιν, καὶ δοξάσατε τὸν θεὸν ἐν τοῖς μέλεσιν ὑμῶν, αὐτὸς ἐγὼ ἐν τῷ σώματι οὐδὲν ἔχων ἀγαθόν; ἀλλ' οὐκ ἔστι τοιοῦτος, οὐκ ἔστιν· μὴ γένοιτο· τέκνον γὰρ ὀργῆς καὶ σκεῦος ὀργῆς πρίν, μεταβαλὼν τὸν τρόπον οὐ τὴν φύσιν, ἐγένετο τίμιον ἐκλογῆς σκεῦος.
thought_title: Paul speaks in a substituted persona, not as himself
orientation: Didymus opens his commentary on Romans 7 by arguing that Paul's words about the wretched man and indwelling sin are spoken in a borrowed character, not about Paul himself or any Christian buried with Christ in baptism.
pass_a_gloss: The divine apostle became an unspotted image of good works for those being taught, for which reason he also cried out: 'Become imitators of me, just as I also am of Christ.' Therefore it is not his own in the proper sense what he said: 'But I know that good does not dwell in my flesh,' nor indeed the 'Wretched man that I am, who will rescue me from the body of this death?' But these things and as many such things he says, speaking in character in a substituted persona, for the refutation of those who love sin. Just as the divine scripture knows to call human beings fleshly, soulish, spiritual, and by countless other names from their own actions, so indeed it knows to call the devil not only Satan and adversary and devil and serpent and lion and Beliar, but also flesh and law and sin and death; for to these we were enslaved through disobedience and not to Christ. For which reason he says: 'When we were in the flesh,' making clear that they are no longer in flesh, although they are in flesh, as therefore not slandering the flesh which we wear around us, but the flesh called by the same name as it, from which we also were set free because we died in Christ through being buried with him through baptism. Truly from this flesh we were set free; for he brings in, saying: 'But now we have been released from the law of sin, having died to that in which we were held, so that we serve in newness of spirit and not oldness of letter.' Then thus he began again the hypothetical speaking in character, beginning from 'What then shall we say? Is the law sin? May it not be!' until 'Wretched man that I am, who will rescue me from the body of this death?' Having set forth an unshaken foundation in a prologue, his own defense, saying thus: 'What then? Is the law sin? May it not be,' and that 'the law is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good.' Here he says law, not the one warring against the law of our mind, but the one that admonishes beforehand, the one that punishes those who sin. For which reason he also voted together with it as holy and just and good. Then thus he began again to explain in sequence what he had said above, having prefaced a word of thanksgiving thus: 'I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord.' Then for the condemnation of those who take occasion from such things and speak evil of the flesh which we wear around us, he says interrogatively: 'So then do I myself with the mind serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin?' Am I, Paul, divided, serving the law of God in one respect, but the law of sin in another? Do I have Christ and Beliar at the same time and in the same place in myself? Do I, the one saying: 'I no longer live, but Christ lives in me,' having lied, have sin living in myself? The one who addressed others: 'Do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit in you, and glorify God in your members,' do I myself have nothing good in my body? But he is not such, he is not; may it not be; for a child of wrath and a vessel of wrath before, having changed his manner, not his nature, he became a precious vessel of election.

choices.english: speaking in character in a substituted persona
choices.why: The glossary requires 'substituted persona' for παρενθέτῳ προσώπῳ and 'speaking in character' for προσωποποιΐα; here the participle ὑποκρινόμενος carries the same sense of playing a part, so 'speaking in character' preserves the rhetorical force.

choices.english: flesh and law and sin and death
choices.why: The glossary fixes these four terms as names for the devil; using the bare English equivalents preserves the homonymy Didymus is arguing for, without adding interpretive glosses.
rejected: sinful nature and law and sin personified and death
the flesh, the law, sin, and death

choices.why: The glossary renders προσωποποιΐα as 'speaking in character'; καθ' ὑπόθεσιν marks the rhetorical device as hypothetical, so the full phrase keeps both elements.
This rare compound describes the law's preparatory, warning function before punishment; rendering it as a relative clause keeps the sense clear without inventing a technical term.
rejected: the one that gives prior warning

choices.term: συνεψηφίσατο αὐτῷ ὡς ὁσίῳ καὶ δικαίῳ καὶ ἀγαθῷ
choices.english: he also voted together with it as holy and just and good
choices.why: The verb συμψηφίζομαι means to cast one's vote along with, i.e., to agree by vote; keeping the voting metaphor preserves Didymus's image of Paul joining in a verdict about the law.
rejected: he also reckoned it as holy and just and good

choices.term: μεταβαλὼν τὸν τρόπον οὐ τὴν φύσιν
choices.english: having changed his manner, not his nature
choices.why: Didymus contrasts τρόπος (manner, way of life) with φύσις (nature) to argue that Paul's conversion changed his conduct, not his created nature; the rendering keeps the antithesis sharp.
rejected: having changed his way, not his essence

pass_b_english: By doing good works the divine apostle became an unspotted image for his disciples. That is why he also cried out: “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1). So what he said is not literally about himself: “I know that good does not dwell in my flesh” (Romans 7:18), nor “Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?” (Romans 7:24). Rather, he says these things and all such things in a substituted persona, speaking in character to refute those who love sin.

Just as divine Scripture knows how to call human beings fleshly, soulish, spiritual, and by countless other names based on their own actions, so too it knows how to call the devil not only Satan, the Adversary, the devil, the Serpent, the Lion, and Beliar, but also flesh and law and sin and death. For we were enslaved to these through disobedience, and not to Christ. That is why he says: “When we were in the flesh” (Romans 7:5), making clear that they are no longer in the flesh, even though they are in the flesh. So he is not slandering the flesh we wear, but the flesh called by the same name, from which we have also been set free because we died in Christ by being buried together with him through baptism. We have truly been freed from this flesh. For he adds: “But now we have been released from the law of sin, having died to that which held us captive, so that we serve in newness of the Spirit and not in oldness of the letter” (Romans 7:6).

Then he began again the hypothetical speaking in character, starting from “What then shall we say? Is the law sin? By no means!” (Romans 7:7) up to “Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?” (Romans 7:24). He laid down an unshaken foundation in his prologue, defending himself by saying: “What then? Is the law sin? By no means!” (Romans 7:7), and that “the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good” (Romans 7:12). Here he means by “law” not the one warring against the law of our mind, but the one that warns beforehand, the one that punishes those who sin. That is why he also agreed with it as holy and just and good.

Then he began again to explain in sequence what he had said earlier, prefacing it with a word of thanksgiving: “I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:25). Then, to condemn those who take occasion from such things and revile the flesh we wear, he asks in the form of a question: “So then, do I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin?” Is Paul himself divided, serving the law of God in one part and the law of sin in another? Do I have Christ and Beliar in myself at the same time and in the same place? Do I, who say “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20), have sin living in me, having lied? I who proclaimed to others: “Do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit within you?” (1 Corinthians 6:19), and “Glorify God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:20), do I myself have nothing good in my body? But Paul is not such a person; he is not. By no means! For though he was formerly a child of wrath and a vessel of wrath, having changed his manner, not his nature, he became a precious vessel of election.

problems.quote: “So then, do I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin?” (Romans 7:25)
problems.source_quote: the question appears after the thanksgiving and is not Romans 7:25 in the standard text; Romans 7:25 is a thanksgiving, not a question.
problems.why: The passage cited as Romans 7:25 is actually a different verse; the question is not Romans 7:25.
problems.fix: cite the correct verse (e.g., Romans 7:24 or indicate it as Didymus’s own quotation without a verse number).
problems.ruling: Greek ἐπερωτηματικῶς introduces a question; the thanksgiving is Rom 7:25a, the question is 7:25b, but the citation format conflates them misleadingly.
